paragraphs: LBOX OPEN addresses the shortage of large, varied datasets for studying legal language outside English. It brings together a Korean legal text collection and tasks covering classification, judgment prediction, and summarization. The corpus contains 147,000 precedents and 259 million tokens, including substantial representation from lower courts where factual issues are reviewed.

The tasks test different connections between legal facts and legal outcomes. Classification models predict case names or relevant statutes from case descriptions. Criminal judgment prediction asks for ranges of fines and imprisonment, while civil prediction asks how much of a claim is accepted given the facts and requested relief. Summarization pairs Supreme Court precedents with their summaries.

The benchmark also includes variants with uncommon case categories and longer documents, expanding the situations that models must handle. Alongside the datasets, the authors introduce LCUBE, a Korean legal language model trained on the collected corpus. Together, these resources provide a shared basis for evaluating several kinds of Korean legal language processing and broadening multilingual legal research.
neurips-2022-a-multi-task-benchmark-for-.tldr: LBOX OPEN introduces a large Korean legal corpus, multiple evaluation tasks, and a language model trained on that corpus.

paragraphs: This paper develops private methods for identifying central regions and representative points in high-dimensional data. It takes a middle position between making no assumptions about the data distribution and requiring a specific, restrictive distribution family. Under mild distributional assumptions, its algorithms use polynomially many samples to estimate quantiles and find or sample points with high Tukey depth.

The central geometric object is the floating body, a convex region that extends the idea of an interquantile range to multiple dimensions. The authors connect robustness results from convex geometry to differential privacy. Their first construction uses the robustness of the floating body's Steiner point to privately return an approximate interior point, representing a typical location within the distribution.

A second construction approximately samples uniformly from the floating body. It uses a private, noisy projection oracle and requires polynomially more samples than finding an interior point. The contribution is therefore both statistical and geometric: properties that make a central region robust also support private access to that region under the paper's distributional assumptions.
neurips-2022-archimedes-meets-privacy-on.tldr: Convex geometry enables private estimation and sampling of central regions in high dimensions under mild distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates mathematical writing into precise statements and proofs that formal systems can process. This paper investigates whether large language models can help with that translation. Its central result concerns formal specifications: the models correctly translate 25.3% of the mathematical competition problems studied into Isabelle/HOL, showing that a meaningful portion of these informal statements can be formalized automatically.

The authors then use the automatically formalized theorems as training material for an existing neural theorem prover. This connects two stages of mathematical automation. A language model converts informal problems into formal statements, and a theorem prover learns from those statements to improve its ability to produce proofs.

On the MiniF2F benchmark, this methodology raises the proof rate from 29.6% to 35.2%, which the paper reports as a new state of the art. The findings support autoformalization as a useful source of training material for theorem proving. They also distinguish successful statement translation from proof production: the translation result supplies theorems, while the downstream evaluation measures how often the prover solves problems.
neurips-2022-autoformalization-with-larg.tldr: Language models correctly formalize some competition mathematics problems, and training on those statements improves a neural theorem prover.

paragraphs: Clustering should remain useful when an input point is missing. This paper studies that requirement for Euclidean clustering, where the objective is to choose k centers minimizing a sum of powered distances to the nearest center. It measures stability through average sensitivity: how much the distribution of an algorithm's output changes, in total variation distance, when a randomly selected input point is deleted.

The authors show that k-means++ and its D-to-the-ell sampling variant have low average sensitivity. They also establish a broader transformation: any approximation algorithm for this clustering objective can be converted into one with low average sensitivity while nearly retaining its approximation guarantee. This links stability to solution quality without requiring a particular starting algorithm.

The analysis also yields algorithms for points arriving online in random order. In the consistent setting, the aim is to preserve a good clustering while changing the maintained solution infrequently. In the dynamic setting, the aim is to keep average update costs low. These results concern average deletion sensitivity and random-order arrivals, rather than an unrestricted guarantee against every possible disruption.
neurips-2022-average-sensitivity-of-eucl.tldr: The paper proves stability guarantees for Euclidean clustering and shows how to add low average sensitivity while nearly preserving approximation quality.

paragraphs: Self-training reduces the need for labeled examples by repeatedly assigning model-generated labels to unlabeled data. Those pseudo labels can be wrong, and training on them can reinforce earlier errors. The authors' experiments identify bias arising both from the semi-supervised problem itself and from inappropriate use of potentially incorrect pseudo labels.

Debiased Self-Training addresses this feedback in two ways. Separate classifier heads, with independent parameters, generate and consume pseudo labels, preventing direct error accumulation between those roles. The method also constructs a worst-case labeling function that remains accurate on labeled examples while making as many mistakes as possible on unlabeled ones. It then adversarially trains the representations to avoid that unfavorable case.

The paper reports average improvements of 6.3% over state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks and 18.9% over FixMatch across 13 diverse tasks. It also finds that incorporating DST into other self-training methods can stabilize training and improve balance across classes. These benefits are reported both for models trained from scratch and for models fine-tuned from pretrained starting points.
neurips-2022-debiased-self-training-for-.tldr: DST separates pseudo-label generation from use and trains against worst-case labeling bias to improve and stabilize semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine multiple neural networks to improve predictions and uncertainty estimates. Deep Combinatorial Aggregation extends this idea by creating multiple versions of network components and combining them in different ways. The resulting combinations supply diverse model proposals and predictions, making the choice of component size a central part of the approach.

The authors find that coarse component choices can outperform conventional deep ensembles in both predictive performance and uncertainty estimation. With finer components, they introduce Deep Combinatorial Weight Averaging, which averages parameterizations to improve baseline training. Its reported performance is comparable to stochastic weight averaging, while avoiding a custom training schedule or changes to BatchNorm layers.

The paper also introduces a loss that encourages consistency and helps train both the weight-averaging approach and modelwise DCA. Experiments cover image classification within the training domain, under distribution shifts, and on out-of-distribution inputs. These results support component recombination as a useful extension of ensemble learning, with different benefits emerging depending on how finely the networks are divided.
neurips-2022-deep-combinatorial-aggregat.tldr: Combining alternative network components improves uncertainty-aware learning, while a related weight-averaging method improves ordinary training.

paragraphs: This paper provides a general way to turn an online convex optimization algorithm into a private stochastic convex optimization algorithm. The starting algorithm must have regret growing at most on the order of the square root of T. The conversion then produces an epsilon-differentially private method for smooth losses, connecting online learning guarantees to private optimization guarantees.

The resulting convergence rate is optimal at the stated order: a term proportional to one over the square root of T, plus a privacy term proportional to one over epsilon times T, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The reduction runs in linear time. Its significance is that privacy can be incorporated through a general conversion, directly paralleling the classical online-to-batch approach without privacy.

The authors also apply their techniques to adaptive online algorithms. This yields private counterparts whose rates depend on variances or parameter norms that need not be known beforehand. The result therefore supports both a general conversion and adaptation to problem characteristics, while retaining the stated requirements on convexity, smoothness, and the starting algorithm's regret.
neurips-2022-differentially-private-onli.tldr: A linear-time reduction converts suitable online convex learners into private optimizers with optimal convergence rates for smooth losses.

paragraphs: Retinal ganglion cells form distinct functional types, each arranging its receptive fields into a mosaic that covers visual space. This paper asks how those mosaics could emerge from efficient coding: the principle that neural systems preserve information about stimuli while limiting metabolic costs. The authors study natural videos while varying the number of simulated output cells available for encoding.

As this channel capacity increases, existing mosaics become denser until critical points are reached and additional cell types appear. Successive types respond to increasingly high temporal frequencies and combine signals across larger spatial areas. The model thus links the available number of cells to both the density of visual coverage and the emergence of functional diversity.

The paper also analyzes how noise affects the relative positions of mosaics belonging to different cell types. Theory and simulations show a transition from alignment to anti-alignment as output noise increases and input noise decreases. Together, these findings provide an efficient-coding account of how capacity and noise can shape retinal organization, offering a possible explanation for the diversity of retinal cell types.
neurips-2022-efficient-coding-channel-ca.tldr: An efficient-coding model links retinal capacity and noise to mosaic density, the emergence of cell types, and their spatial arrangement.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a distribution's entropy while using only a constant number of memory words. The distribution has an alphabet of size k, and the estimator processes independent samples drawn from that same distribution. The goal is an estimate within an additive error of epsilon, making both sample requirements and memory usage central to the problem.

Earlier work achieved this accuracy using a sample count proportional to k divided by epsilon cubed, multiplied by factors polynomial in the logarithm of one over epsilon. The new scheme improves the main dependence to k divided by epsilon squared, again with such logarithmic factors. It retains constant memory while reducing the number of observations needed as the requested accuracy becomes more demanding.

The contribution is therefore an improvement in sample efficiency under the same severe storage constraint. The alphabet size remains a linear factor in the stated sample bound. The authors conjecture that their dependence is optimal up to the logarithmic factors; the abstract presents this optimality as a conjecture, rather than an established matching lower bound.
neurips-2022-estimation-of-entropy-in-co.tldr: A constant-memory entropy estimator improves the main sample dependence from k/epsilon³ to k/epsilon², with logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Training-data influence methods try to identify which examples shape a model's behavior. For large language models, following influence through every parameter can be computationally impractical, so methods often examine only the final layer. This paper identifies a cancellation effect there: shared representations can produce large, opposing influence contributions that make the resulting scores less discriminative.

The proposed TracIn-WE method adapts TracIn to operate on the word embedding layer, where the authors find less severe cancellation. Although embeddings might appear too low-level to capture the relevant behavior, the method uses gradients rather than embeddings alone. The authors find that these gradients retain useful information, possibly because their computation passes through the higher layers.

Across three language classification tasks and different models, TracIn-WE significantly outperforms influence methods applied to the final layer in case-deletion evaluations. Such evaluations test whether removing examples identified as influential changes model behavior. The method also assigns influence scores to individual words within training inputs, providing a more detailed way to inspect and debug the data behind a prediction.
neurips-2022-first-is-better-than-last-f.tldr: Measuring influence through embedding-layer gradients reduces cancellation and better identifies consequential language training examples in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning starts from a pretrained model and adapts it to a target dataset. The paper revisits evidence that, in some vision tasks with more training examples, training from scratch can match this strategy. It analyzes the phenomenon using an excess-risk bound and finds that the bound may depend only weakly on the pretrained model.

That observation motivates using the pretraining examples themselves during fine-tuning, alongside the model they produced. The analysis shows that including appropriate pretraining data can improve the target task's excess-risk bound. The qualification matters: the result motivates choosing useful source examples, rather than assuming that any additional pretraining data will help.

The authors turn this motivation into a strategy for selecting a subset of the pretraining dataset to include during fine-tuning. Experiments on eight image classification benchmarks support the effectiveness of the resulting pipeline. The approach assumes access to pretraining data during adaptation and treats data selection as part of transfer learning, extending the usual emphasis on transferring a model's learned parameters.
neurips-2022-improved-fine-tuning-by-bet.tldr: Selecting suitable pretraining examples for reuse during fine-tuning can improve target-task generalization, supported by analysis and image classification experiments.

paragraphs: Point cloud classification learns about three-dimensional objects from collections of points. This paper supplements that learning with two-dimensional views, which can contain appearance information such as color, texture, and shading. Its PointCMT training strategy uses rendered or projected images of an object to improve the representation learned by a point cloud model.

The approach treats this transfer as knowledge distillation within a teacher-student framework. Feature and classifier enhancement criteria address differences between the image and point cloud modalities and aim to avoid harmful transfer. The resulting improvement is to a point-only representation, and the method does not require changes to the point cloud network's architecture.

Experiments cover multiple datasets and network backbones. The paper reports significant gains and state-of-the-art results with PointCMT-equipped PointNet++ and PointMLP, including 94.4% accuracy on ModelNet40 and 86.7% on ScanObjectNN. The findings show that auxiliary image information during training can improve point cloud classification while preserving the underlying architecture, making cross-modal supervision useful beyond models that directly combine both input types.
neurips-2022-let-images-give-you-more-po.tldr: PointCMT distills information from object images into point cloud models, improving classification without modifying their architectures.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether diffusion models can benefit from a flexible nonlinear diffusion process that adapts to data. Its Implicit Nonlinear Diffusion Model combines a normalizing flow with diffusion. Instead of directly specifying nonlinear diffusion in the original data space, it applies linear diffusion in a latent space connected to the data by the flow network.

The learned flow determines the resulting nonlinearity in data space. This makes the diffusion process adjustable through the mapping between the two spaces. The authors describe DDPM++ as a restricted version of this construction in which the flow is fixed to the identity mapping, removing that source of flexibility.

The paper reports that this flexibility gives INDM a learning curve approaching maximum-likelihood estimation, compared with the non-MLE curve of DDPM++. It also reports robustness when the diffusion process is discretized for sampling. In image-generation experiments, INDM reaches an FID of 1.75 on CelebA, described as state of the art. These findings support the value of learning the space in which diffusion takes place.
neurips-2022-maximum-likelihood-training.tldr: INDM learns a flow that turns latent linear diffusion into data-adaptive nonlinear diffusion, improving training behavior and reported image-generation quality.

paragraphs: Lifelong reinforcement learning aims to reuse experience across a sequence of tasks. This paper proposes a model-based approach that learns a hierarchical Bayesian posterior capturing structure shared by related tasks. It combines that learned distribution with sampling-based Bayesian exploration to improve how efficiently the agent gathers experience across the task family.

The theoretical analysis begins with finite Markov decision processes. It relates the number of samples needed for learning to the quality of the posterior's initialization. This connects the usefulness of previously acquired knowledge to subsequent learning efficiency, giving a formal basis for carrying information between tasks through the posterior.

To handle continuous states, the authors introduce Variational Bayesian Lifelong Reinforcement Learning, which can work with recent model-based deep reinforcement learning methods. The algorithm exhibits backward transfer, meaning later learning can improve performance on earlier tasks. Experiments across several challenging domains report better forward and backward transfer than state-of-the-art lifelong methods. The results support a shared Bayesian model as a way to help both upcoming and previously encountered tasks.
neurips-2022-model-based-lifelong-reinfo.tldr: A shared Bayesian model and sampling-based exploration improve learning efficiency and transfer across related reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Many variance-reduction methods track one changing function during optimization. This paper studies a harder situation: tracking many function blocks when each iteration can inspect only a constant number of them. The setting arises in objectives built by summing composed functions, where the inner functions are available only through noisy evaluations and derivative information.

The proposed Multi-block-Single-probe Variance Reduced estimator, or MSVR, adapts the idea behind STORM to this restricted-access setting. Its customized correction term addresses errors associated with both sampled blocks and blocks left unobserved in the current iteration. The key challenge is therefore maintaining a useful estimate of the whole collection despite receiving only a small amount of fresh information.

Using MSVR, the authors develop algorithms with improved complexity guarantees across nonconvex, convex, strongly convex, and Polyak–Łojasiewicz objectives. The improvements include sample-complexity orders and dependence on the strong-convexity parameter. Experiments on multitask deep AUC maximization also report better performance with the estimator. Together, the theory and experiments support variance reduction tailored to partially observed collections of functions.
neurips-2022-multi-block-single-probe-va.tldr: MSVR tracks many changing function blocks from few observations per iteration, improving guarantees for coupled compositional optimization.

paragraphs: Interactive imitation learning lets a learner request expert annotations while learning sequential decisions. This paper examines classification-based online imitation learning, focusing on the general non-realizable case, where the chosen policy class need not perfectly represent the expert. It asks which regret guarantees can be achieved by algorithms that efficiently use optimization oracles.

The first result rules out a broad approach: proper online algorithms, which remain within the original policy class, cannot guarantee sublinear regret in general. The authors respond with Logger, an improper learning framework built around a new mixed policy class. Logger reduces the imitation-learning problem to online linear optimization, expanding the available algorithmic tools.

Within this framework, two oracle-efficient algorithms offer different tradeoffs between sample requirements and interaction rounds, with improvements over behavior cloning. The paper also establishes a boundary: under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, efficient dynamic-regret minimization is infeasible within Logger. The contribution combines constructive guarantees with impossibility results, clarifying both the value of mixed policies and the limits of stronger performance requirements.
neurips-2022-on-efficient-online-imitati.tldr: Logger uses mixed policies to enable efficient online imitation learning while the paper establishes limits for proper learners and dynamic regret.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much data is needed to learn a multiclass predictor that remains reliable under adversarial perturbations. It works within the Probably Approximately Correct learning framework. The authors first show that two dimensions used to characterize ordinary multiclass learning, graph dimension and Natarajan dimension, do not serve the same role directly in the robust setting.

They introduce adversarial versions of these quantities: AG-dimension and AN-dimension. The former supports an upper bound on robust learning's sample complexity, while the latter supports a lower bound. These bounds connect properties of the predictor class under adversarial changes to the amount of training data sufficient or required for learning.

For linear multiclass predictors, the paper calculates both adversarial dimensions and shows that each has the same order as its ordinary counterpart. It also proves that AG-dimension and AN-dimension are not equivalent in general. The results supply complexity measures suited to robustness while showing why the upper-bound and lower-bound measures cannot simply be treated as interchangeable descriptions of every learning problem.
neurips-2022-on-robust-multiclass-learna.tldr: Adversarial graph and Natarajan dimensions provide upper and lower sample-complexity bounds for robust multiclass learning.

paragraphs: Temporal graph networks represent interactions that change over time. This paper compares two major approaches: aggregating temporal walks and combining local message passing with recurrent memory. Its theoretical constructions show that neither family contains the other's representational abilities. Each can distinguish some situations that the other cannot, so neither provides a universally stronger foundation.

The authors extend the Weisfeiler–Leman graph test to temporal graphs and connect it to message-passing networks. With injective updates, which preserve distinctions between different inputs, these networks reach the expressive power of the temporal test. The analysis also shows that sufficiently deep message-passing networks gain no additional expressiveness from memory, and that both studied families fail to compute properties such as girth.

These findings motivate PINT, an architecture combining injective temporal message passing with relative positional features. The paper proves that PINT is more expressive than both original families and reports significant improvements over existing temporal graph networks on several real-world benchmarks. The work thus turns representational limits into concrete architectural choices supported by both proofs and empirical results.
neurips-2022-provably-expressive-tempora.tldr: PINT combines injective temporal message passing and relative positions to exceed the proven expressiveness of two major temporal graph network families.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning often trains agents centrally but requires them to act separately. Individual Global Max decomposition helps connect these stages by aligning local decisions with the joint policy. This paper examines a potential weakness in that connection: the decomposition loses information, and the resulting error accumulates in methods based on hypernetworks.

The proposed remedy uses imitation learning to separate the lossy decomposition from Bellman iterations, the repeated value-learning updates. This separation is intended to keep decomposition error from repeatedly feeding into those updates. The method addresses how centralized learning is translated into decentralized behavior, rather than focusing only on satisfying the consistency condition between local and joint policies.

The authors provide theoretical support for the strategy and evaluate it on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge under a zero-sight-view setting. They report that it outperforms state-of-the-art IGM-based methods in that evaluation. The contribution highlights that consistency of decisions does not by itself eliminate information loss, and that isolating the decomposition step can avoid the identified accumulation of error.
neurips-2022-rethinking-individual-globa.tldr: Separating lossy policy decomposition from Bellman updates through imitation learning avoids identified error accumulation in cooperative multi-agent learning.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness requires a model to preserve its predictions around natural inputs despite small perturbations. The paper starts from the observation that model capacity can be insufficient for this demand, and that ensembles can help. However, majority voting can discard a correct prediction when only a minority of the component models produce it.

Synergy-of-Experts replaces this voting-based approach with a collaboration scheme. Each component model focuses on a particular area of vulnerability, leaving other areas to the remaining components. This division aims to use the available model capacity more effectively. It also allows the combined system to produce a correct answer even when only one component is correct, without claiming that one correct component always guarantees success.

Experiments compare the method with various ensemble approaches under white-box and transfer-based adversarial attacks. The reported results favor Synergy-of-Experts. They support the idea that how component models divide responsibility and combine their outputs can matter for robustness, beyond simply having several models available to vote on the same input.
neurips-2022-synergy-of-experts-collabor.tldr: Synergy-of-Experts assigns models different vulnerability areas and combines them collaboratively to improve reported adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search treats network design as an algorithmic task. To reason about candidate networks, the search system needs a representation of the architecture itself. This paper focuses on that representation problem: how to encode a network design so that an automated system can model it and distinguish it from other designs.

TA-GATES is a graph-based encoding scheme that represents an architecture through a process analogous to its training. The central methodological choice is to make the encoding reflect the training process explicitly. This connects the representation of a candidate architecture to the process that will ultimately determine how that candidate learns.

The authors report extensive experiments showing that TA-GATES offers flexibility and discriminative power that improve architecture modeling. Better modeling matters because it supports the broader effort to explore new network designs automatically and understand automated design decisions. The authors also expect explicit modeling of training to help wider automated deep learning systems; that broader benefit is presented as an expectation, beyond the stated experimental finding about architecture representations.
neurips-2022-ta-gates-an-encoding-scheme.tldr: TA-GATES improves neural architecture modeling with a graph-based encoding designed to mirror the network training process.

paragraphs: A model that meets fairness goals in its training environment may lose those properties when deployed elsewhere. This paper studies that transfer problem across different kinds of distribution shift. Its analysis finds domain shifts more challenging than subpopulation shifts, showing that the nature of the environmental change matters when assessing whether fairness will persist.

Drawing inspiration from self-training methods that transfer accuracy across domains, the authors derive a sufficient condition for transferring group fairness. They use that condition to design an algorithm centered on fair consistency regularization. The theoretical result supplies a route under which fairness transfer is supported; it does not state that the condition is necessary for every successful transfer.

The authors build a synthetic benchmark covering diverse shifts to examine the theoretical findings. They also evaluate the method on real image and tabular datasets. The experiments show effective transfer of both fairness and accuracy across various shifts. Together, the analysis and results support treating fairness preservation as an explicit adaptation objective when a model moves between environments.
neurips-2022-transferring-fairness-under.tldr: A sufficient condition for fairness transfer motivates a consistency-regularized algorithm that preserves fairness and accuracy across tested distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Graph models can perform unevenly across nodes with different numbers of connections. In particular, graph convolutional networks often perform worse on low-degree nodes. This paper examines that structural fairness issue in graph contrastive learning and finds that its learned representations already show less degree bias than those learned by graph convolutional networks.

The theoretical explanation concerns the arrangement of communities in the representation space. Graph contrastive learning concentrates nodes within the same community and separates different communities. This clearer structure moves low-degree nodes away from community boundaries, connecting improved fairness to the geometry of the learned representations.

The authors use this analysis to develop GRADE, a graph augmentation method that applies different strategies to low-degree and high-degree nodes. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and evaluation protocols support its effectiveness. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation of an existing advantage and a method designed around that explanation. Here fairness specifically concerns performance differences associated with graph degree, so the finding addresses structural disadvantage within graph learning.
neurips-2022-uncovering-the-structural-f.tldr: Graph contrastive learning reduces degree bias through clearer community structure, motivating GRADE's degree-dependent graph augmentation.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation needs labels for individual pixels, which makes adding new classes expensive. This paper studies a setting where existing classes have pixel-level annotations, while new classes have only image-level labels. Its goal is to transfer useful segmentation knowledge from the richly annotated classes so the new classes can be learned with cheaper supervision.

The framework builds on MaskFormer and separates each proposal into a single-label classification problem and a binary segmentation problem. It transfers two kinds of similarity. Proposal-to-pixel similarity supports learning masks for new classes, while pixel-to-pixel similarity learned from existing classes supplies class-independent semantic relationships across images.

Those pixel relationships are distilled into the new classes' masks to regularize segmentation learning. A complementary loss further supports learning the new classes. Experiments on COCO-Stuff-10K and ADE20K demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The approach matters because it transfers information about spatial and semantic relationships, allowing detailed annotations from existing categories to support mask learning for categories that have only image-level supervision.
neurips-2022-weak-shot-semantic-segmenta.tldr: Transferring proposal-to-pixel and pixel-to-pixel similarities helps learn segmentation masks for new classes with only image-level labels.

paragraphs: ZSON trains a virtual agent to find objects described in language without using object-navigation rewards or demonstrations. Instead, it learns image-goal navigation: reaching the place where a supplied picture was captured. The approach represents goal images in a semantic space that also accommodates language, enabling training in unannotated three-dimensional environments.

After training, a textual object request is projected into that same space and supplied as the goal. The shared representation connects the visual goals used during learning with the language goals used for object search. Zero-shot here refers to transferring into object-goal navigation without task-specific rewards or demonstrations; the navigation behavior itself is learned through the image-goal task.

Evaluations on Gibson, HM3D, and MP3D show absolute success improvements of 4.2% to 20.0% over existing zero-shot methods. The authors also observe generalization to compound requests that either name a room or imply one through a combination of objects. These findings support shared image-language goal representations as a scalable route to open-world object navigation.
neurips-2022-zson-zero-shot-object-goal-.tldr: ZSON transfers image-goal navigation to language-directed object search through shared multimodal goal embeddings, without object-navigation rewards or demonstrations.
